title: The stability class of the global overturning circulation

concept.text: The proposed innovation is to determine whether the modern ocean’s major overturning cells have one persistent circulation state or can sustain alternative states under the same specified background conditions. It would classify the Atlantic and Antarctic cells separately while accounting for their connections within the global ocean. The result would be expressed through measurable ocean properties and tested against models, including models that resolve vigorous ocean eddies.

Monostability means that only one stable state exists within the conditions being considered; bistability means that two stable states can persist under those same conditions. A much weaker circulation could therefore remain after the disturbance that initiated it has subsided. These classifications depend on the background climate and forcing range. Monostability does not guarantee that circulation changes smoothly, and bistability does not establish that realistic future disturbances can reach the weaker state.

The research problem arises from palaeoclimate evidence suggesting abrupt switches between stronger and weaker Atlantic circulation during recent glacial cycles, together with disagreement among models exposed to the same imposed freshwater forcing. Those findings motivate a determination of modern stability; they do not themselves classify the present ocean. An observable warning of approaching change and a demonstrated classification of alternative persistent states are related but distinct achievements.

significance.text: A successful determination would establish a qualitative physical property of a major component of Earth’s climate system: whether substantially different persistent circulation states are available under specified modern conditions. That would strengthen the physical basis for assessing persistent ocean change and interpreting disagreements among models, rather than treating every simulated weakening or collapse as evidence of the same underlying stability regime.

The direct consequence would be knowledge of which stable states exist within the tested conditions. Establishing whether plausible heat and freshwater forcing can actually trigger a transition would additionally require forcing thresholds, trajectories and recovery times. The 2025 review explicitly allows that realistic freshwater input might be insufficient to cause a transition. Describing a shutdown as irreversible would also require specifying which forcing changes are reversed and over what timescale recovery is assessed.

Conditional downstream benefits include better founded assessments of regional weather, sea ice and carbon-cycle changes associated with persistent circulation weakening. The review already discusses impact simulations and identifies reduced Antarctic overturning as a mechanism that reduces the efficiency of the global ocean carbon sink. Stability classification alone would neither quantify those consequences nor establish when they would occur; additional coupled climate and biogeochemical analysis would remain necessary.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is an observationally usable stability diagnostic whose interpretation survives changes in model formulation and resolution. It must distinguish alternative persistent states from temporary weakening and connect observable circulation and freshwater properties to the feedbacks that maintain or destabilize the circulation. The supplied evidence motivates developing observable precursors, but does not establish that a clean diagnostic capable of classifying stability exists.

A central scientific barrier is explaining why the same freshwater perturbation produces an off state or a much weaker Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, or AMOC, in some models but not others. Freshwater balance, background state and coupled feedbacks all matter. Other feedbacks can temporarily mask or overcome the salt-advection feedback and alter stability, so improved turbulent mixing or a more accurate freshwater budget alone cannot settle the classification.

The resolution barrier requires appropriate stability experiments in strongly eddying climate models, a gap identified in the 2025 review. The Antarctic problem requires its own treatment: evidence for possible tipping does not supply either a settled threshold or an observational stability diagnostic. Its classification cannot simply be inherited from conclusions about the AMOC.

Proposed engineering requirements include experiments long enough to separate transient adjustment from persistent states, explicit equilibration and persistence definitions, and uncertainty estimates that connect model diagnostics to imperfect observations. The design must also specify how a change in one overturning cell affects classification of the other. These are requirements for a convincing research program, not capabilities demonstrated by the supplied material.

current_state.text: Loriani and coauthors’ review, published on 8 October 2025 in Earth System Dynamics, volume 16, pages 1611–1653, documents AMOC tipping across a hierarchy of ocean–climate models. Section 2.1.1, printed page 1617, identifies very high resolution, strongly eddying climate models as the remaining category in which appropriate experiments had not yet been conducted. This is a dated assessment of model experiments, not a demonstration that the actual modern ocean has a particular stability class.

The same review cautions on printed page 1615 that expecting tipping within a few decades is not sufficiently substantiated. Its abstract identifies evidence for possible collapse of the AMOC, the North Atlantic subpolar gyre and Antarctic overturning under warmer and fresher conditions. These are distinct circulation systems; evidence of possible collapse across them does not establish a shared diagnostic, common threshold or common transition date. The Utrecht page supplies the abstract of this same review, rather than independent corroborating research.

The supplied review assessment locates discussion of the latest IPCC assessment on printed pages 1614 and 1618, correcting the earlier research note that this discussion could not be found. Loriani and coauthors interpret that assessment as leaving open the possibility of AMOC collapse within the next century. This establishes what their review says about the IPCC assessment; the underlying IPCC material was not separately inspected in the supplied evidence, and this statement is not a dated collapse prediction.

The research notes attribute a stronger judgment to a Dijkstra-led review reported as accepted on 5 March 2026 and associated with WIREs Climate Change 17(2), e70049: that the evidence for AMOC multistability has broadened and that the present AMOC occupies such a regime. The notes report access to an abstract and title page but a failed PDF fetch. No artifact of that source is retained in the supplied evidence, so its wording, authorship, acceptance date and technical basis cannot be independently verified from this package. This limitation does not establish that the reported conclusion is false. Even if confirmed, a review judgment about the AMOC would require separate assessment against the proposed observable demonstration and would not determine Antarctic stability.

The validated assessment used a partial extraction of the 43-page 2025 article: the retained text was capped at 120,000 characters and ended on PDF page 25, and figures were not visually inspected. The cited passages fall within the reviewed text. The supplied evidence does not demonstrate an observable criterion validated in strongly eddying models for both cells. Because no subsequent-work freshness record was supplied, it also cannot establish whether later research had completed that demonstration by November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: formulate a criterion in measurable ocean quantities and test whether it correctly separates monostable from bistable behavior across a model hierarchy that includes strongly eddying climate models. Establish the stability behavior independently through perturbation and recovery experiments, rather than defining success solely by agreement with the diagnostic being tested. State background conditions, forcing ranges and uncertainty explicitly.
completion_criteria.label: Ocean criterion distinguishes monostability from bistability across strongly eddying models

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: repeat the classification with multiple initial states, freshwater and heat perturbations, and forcing reversal experiments. Report equilibration times, how long alternative states persist, and whether apparent persistence could reflect slow adjustment. Independent implementations and reproducible experimental protocols should test whether the result depends on one model’s formulation. Specific durations and tolerances remain to be justified; none are supplied as established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Stability classification reproduces independently with slow adjustment explicitly assessed

completion_criteria.text: Proposed observational application: apply the validated criterion separately to the Atlantic and Antarctic cells, account for their coupling, and propagate measurement and model uncertainty into each conclusion. An indeterminate observational classification should remain an explicit possible outcome. Any claim that realistic future forcing can trigger persistent shutdown should additionally demonstrate the relevant thresholds, forcing trajectories and recovery behavior.
completion_criteria.label: Separate Atlantic and Antarctic classifications account for coupling and uncertainty

completion_criteria.text: A collapse in one coarse model, an early-warning statistic fitted to a short proxy record, or a review’s multistability conclusion would contribute evidence but would not alone meet this proposed demonstration. Finite experiments would establish the diagnostic’s demonstrated breadth within specified conditions, not literal validity across every possible ocean state or future forcing.
completion_criteria.label: Diagnostic validity is bounded by experimentally demonstrated conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OCE-01, “A closed theory of oceanic turbulent transport,” could improve the representation of mixing and transport used in stability experiments. That would support OCE-07 without by itself establishing the effects of freshwater balance and coupled feedbacks on stability. Only OCE-01’s title is supplied, so the earlier assertion that it can supply the required fluxes remains unverified.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-02, “Synoptic sensing of the ocean interior,” could support measurements needed for an observable diagnostic. OCE-04, “Persistent mobile operations at full ocean depth,” and OCE-10, “Basin-scale underwater positioning without surfacing,” could enable sustained, geographically referenced observations. These concern sensing and operational capabilities; OCE-07 concerns the physical inference made from observations and experiments. Their specific contributions cannot be established from titles alone.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-06, “A verified law of ice-shelf basal melting,” could inform freshwater forcing relevant to Antarctic circulation. OCE-03, “A predictive closure of the biological carbon pump,” and OCE-09, “A predictive theory of pelagic size structure and trophic transfer,” concern biological processes that could help assess consequences of circulation change. None of these titles establishes a solution to overturning stability, and a stability classification would not replace their separate physical or ecological objectives.

Roster-based synthesis: OCE-05, “Closure of ocean–crust fluid and biogeochemical exchange,” addresses exchange across the ocean floor, while OCE-08, “Continuous centimeter-level geodesy of the seismogenic seafloor,” addresses seafloor deformation measurement. The supplied titles establish no direct dependency on either for OCE-07. They remain separate concepts; any specific coupling or shared infrastructure would require their fuller specifications.

change_log.change: Retained OCE-07’s identity and expanded the explanation of monostability, bistability and separate Atlantic and Antarctic classifications.
change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent; clearer definitions distinguish its scientific objective from predictions of collapse.

change_log.change: Replaced the claim that classification directly determines irreversible shutdown under plausible forcing with conditional statements about accessibility, thresholds, trajectories and recovery times.
change_log.reason: Alternative stable states need not be reachable under realistic forcing, and irreversibility requires specified reversal conditions and timescales.

change_log.change: Removed the implication that monostability guarantees smooth weakening.
change_log.reason: The validated review identifies this as an unjustified inference from stability class.

change_log.change: Integrated freshwater balance, competing feedbacks, background-state dependence and model disagreement into the missing breakthrough.
change_log.reason: These mechanisms explain why improved mixing alone cannot settle stability.

change_log.change: Preserved the dated 2025 model-resolution gap and timing caution, and corrected the earlier inability to locate the IPCC discussion.
change_log.reason: The validated review identifies the relevant passages, while supporting only an indirect account of the IPCC assessment.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 2026 review conclusion with explicit attribution and verification limits.
change_log.reason: The absent artifact prevents confirmation but does not justify rejecting the reported result or deleting the concept.

change_log.change: Replaced an unconditional assertion of continued noncompletion with a statement bounded by the supplied evidence.
change_log.reason: The empty freshness record cannot establish the state of subsequent research as of November 2026.

change_log.change: Added proposed reproducibility, perturbation, recovery and uncertainty requirements without inventing numerical thresholds.
change_log.reason: These make the demonstration more concrete while preserving its status as a proposal and acknowledging finite validation.

change_log.change: Explained all supplied roster relationships as title-based synthesis and qualified OCE-01’s asserted contribution.
change_log.reason: The roster provides titles but no specifications sufficient to verify detailed dependencies.

change_log.change: Preserved extraction, figure-access and source-capture limitations in the evidence narrative.
change_log.reason: These limits affect how confidently the supplied review can support conclusions.

unresolved_issues: Whether the reported 2026 Dijkstra-led review has the stated identity, acceptance date, wording and evidentiary basis remains unverified because no artifact is supplied.
Whether subsequent research has demonstrated the proposed criterion in strongly eddying models for both cells is unresolved; no freshness record is supplied.
It remains uncertain whether a sufficiently discriminating observational stability criterion is feasible for either cell.
Forcing ranges, background conditions, equilibration and persistence durations, uncertainty tolerances and treatment of coupled cells remain to be specified.
A stability classification would leave additional questions about realistic triggering, recovery and quantitative climate and ecosystem consequences.
Detailed dependencies on OCE-01 and the other roster entries cannot be verified without their specifications.
The IPCC interpretation is supported through the 2025 review, not through a separately inspected IPCC source.

brief.title: Knowing whether ocean currents can stay weakened
possible: We could tell whether the Atlantic and Antarctic ocean circulation systems can settle into lasting weaker states under the same climate conditions. Measurements would help distinguish a temporary slowdown from a change that persists after the original disturbance ends.
why: Climate scientists would gain a firmer basis for assessing persistent ocean change and understanding why models disagree. That would support better assessments of changes in regional weather, sea ice and the ocean’s uptake of carbon.

sources.showed: Their review found evidence that Atlantic and Antarctic circulation systems may collapse under warmer, less salty conditions. It documented Atlantic tipping across models of differing complexity.
sources.quote:
Some model simulations
have also shown abrupt changes in the Antarctic deep-water
formation (Lago and England, 2019; Li et al., 2023).
sources.cited_for: The review supports investigating whether ocean circulation can sustain lasting alternative states.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a measurement-based test of modern Atlantic and Antarctic stability validated in models with vigorous ocean swirls.

sources.showed: A later version of the same work.
This is a review of evidence that Atlantic circulation can sustain different persistent states under the same background conditions.
sources.cited_for: It addresses whether the present Atlantic circulation has alternative persistent states.
sources.not_established: A review conclusion alone does not demonstrate a measurement-based stability test or determine Antarctic stability.

shown: Loriani and coauthors documented Atlantic circulation tipping across a range of models. Their review identified experiments in models detailed enough to represent vigorous ocean swirls as a remaining gap. Evidence of possible Antarctic collapse also exists, but its stability needs a separate assessment.
missing: A reliable test using measurable ocean properties must distinguish lasting alternative states from temporary weakening.
Experiments must establish stability in models that represent vigorous ocean swirls and explain why models respond differently.
Separate Atlantic and Antarctic assessments must account for their connections and for uncertainty in measurements.

milestones.label: Measurements distinguish lasting circulation states across detailed models
milestones.explanation: A test using measurable ocean properties would have to match independent disturbance and recovery experiments, including models with vigorous ocean swirls. This would establish whether it identifies alternative lasting states.

milestones.label: Independent experiments reproduce the classification after slow adjustment
milestones.explanation: Independent experiments would have to reproduce the result from different starting states, after changes in heat and freshwater and their reversal. This would distinguish lasting states from slow adjustment.

milestones.label: Atlantic and Antarctic assessments account for their connections
milestones.explanation: The validated test would have to assess each system separately, including their connections and measurement and model uncertainty. This would establish what observations can tell us, including an inconclusive result.

milestones.label: The test’s limits match the conditions actually demonstrated
milestones.explanation: Experiments would have to establish the conditions within which the test works. This would keep conclusions within demonstrated limits, since a simulated collapse or warning signal alone cannot establish its reliability.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether measurements can distinguish alternative persistent states reliably in either circulation system.
The climate conditions, disturbance ranges and duration needed to establish persistence remain to be defined.
Even if a weaker stable state exists, realistic future changes might not reach it; triggering conditions and recovery remain separate questions.
